title: Chapter 9: Failover Testing and Game Days: Proving Your SQL Server HA Works

questions.q: What is the safe, supported failover test for RDS Multi-AZ?
options: Terminate the primary EC2 instance
reboot-db-instance --force-failover
Delete and recreate the standby
Block the primary's security group traffic
questions.explain: The chapter states the safe supported test is reboot-db-instance --force-failover, which exercises the real failover path: DNS update, replica promotion, and application reconnect.

questions.q: The chapter says to record three RTO numbers from every test. Which one do users actually experience?
options: Detection time (failure to failover initiation)
Promotion time (failover initiation to new primary accepting writes)
Client recovery time (new primary accepting writes to application fully serving traffic) — always the largest
DNS propagation time alone
questions.explain: The chapter stresses vendor RTO numbers measure the database; client recovery time is always the largest of the three and the only one users feel — instrument it with canary writes.

questions.q: How do game days escalate across quarters?
options: Region drill first, then work down to planned failovers
Only test planned failovers; unplanned tests are too risky
Planned failover → unplanned primary kill → AZ failure simulation → full region drill
Skip to the region drill immediately for maximum realism
questions.explain: The chapter defines four levels: Level 1 planned failover, Level 2 unplanned primary kill, Level 3 AZ impairment, Level 4 region drill — each tests a different failure mode, and only the region drill validates DR rather than HA.

questions.q: After a failover, the database is up but the application is broken. The chapter names the number one cause:
options: Corrupted transaction logs on the new primary
Expired TLS certificates
Wrong RDS parameter group family
Login and SQL Server Agent job drift — logins and jobs live outside the availability group (compare sys.server_principals and msdb.dbo.sysjobs)
questions.explain: The post-failover checklist emphasizes comparing logins and jobs between replicas because they live outside the AG — drift here is the number one cause of 'failover worked but the app is broken.'

questions.q: Why does listener DNS staleness cause partial outages after failover?
options: DNS servers delete the listener record permanently
Java JVMs cache DNS forever by default unless networkaddress.cache.ttl is set, so some app servers keep hitting the dead primary
RDS never updates the endpoint DNS
The AG listener stops resolving after one failover
questions.explain: The chapter describes this as the most confusing partial-outage pattern: JVMs cache DNS forever by default and some pools hold resolved addresses, so a subset of servers hammers the dead primary while others work fine.
